---
title: "Practical work 2"
subtitle: "DAI · A network application with TCP or UDP"
---

## What you will build

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
- A **network application**, in a group: an **application protocol**
  and two Java programs that use it, a **server** and a **client**.
- You define the protocol, and you choose its transport: TCP, UDP, or
  both.
- **You choose what the application does.** A chat, a chess game, a
  shopping list, an Internet of Things (IoT) network simulation…
- Be creative, but reasonable: the point is the protocol and the
  network code.

:::

## Why this project

- Chapter 06: application protocols.
- The TCP & UDP programming chapters, and the Network concurrency
  chapter.
- Chapter 05: package and publish the application with Docker.

## Objectives

- Define an application protocol, in a specification another team could
  implement.
- Implement the protocol as a client and a server, with TCP and/or UDP.
- Serve several clients at the same time.
- Package, publish and run the application with Docker.
- Explain your work, in the README and in front of the class.

## What your application must do

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- Follow an **application protocol you define**, in a specification
  with the four sections of chapter 06. The SMS protocol is a model.
- Two picocli commands: one starts the **server**, the other the
  **client**.
- The client has a **REPL** (Read-Eval-Print Loop): the user types
  commands and reads the answers without leaving the application.
- The server accepts **several clients at the same time**. No idea
  where several clients make sense? Ask us.
- **Packaged with Docker**, published on GitHub Container Registry.
- **Slightly more** than the course examples, and slightly different.
  No need to shoot for the moon.
:::

## Demo 1: file transfer, with TCP

- The server serves the files of its directory; the client lists and
  downloads them in a REPL. Several clients at the same time, with a
  pool of threads.

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{.text filename="Client" code-line-numbers="false"}
> LS
Available files on server:
demo.txt
notes.txt
> GET demo.txt
Downloading file from server...
File saved to demo.txt
> GET not-found.txt
The specified file was not found on the server.
> QUIT
Bye.
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{.text filename="Server" code-line-numbers="false"}
Starting server on port 12345 with thread pool size 4.
New client connected from 127.0.0.1:50943
Client disconnected
```
:::
::::
:::

## Demo 2: weather station, with UDP

- Sensors send their measures to **multicast** groups, fire and
  forget. The weather station receives them, and answers a client in
  **unicast**: all the measures, or their average.

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em"}
```{.text filename="Thermometer" code-line-numbers="false"}
Emitter of type thermometer started (127.0.0.1:9876).
Multicasting measure : 1.0 to 239.0.0.1:9876 on interface en0
Multicasting measure : 38.0 to 239.0.0.1:9876 on interface en0
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.text filename="Weather station" code-line-numbers="false"}
Multicast receiver started (127.0.0.1:9876)
Unicast receiver started (127.0.0.1:1234)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.text filename="Client" code-line-numbers="false"}
> 3
List all measures (1) or only the average? (2)
> 2
Received average: 1003.83
```
:::
::::
:::

## Groups and idea

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
- Groups of **two to three** students. You choose your partners; no
  partner? We assign you one.
- Open a **GitHub Discussion** in the course organization, category
  *Show and tell*:
  - title: `[DAI {{< var year >}} Class <A or C>] PW2 - <first name> <last name>, …`,
  - description: a few lines on what your application will do.
- Do it **before the next course**, even if your idea is not final.
- We use it to plan the presentations, and to tell you early if the
  scope is too small or too large.
:::

## Submission

- Update the Discussion you opened at the start with:
  - the link to your repository,
  - the **commit hash** you want us to grade.
- Due: DAI-TIC-A **Tuesday 01.12, 23:59**; DAI-TIC-C **Monday
  07.12, 23:59**.
- The penalties are in the rules.

## Presentations

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- DAI-TIC-A: **Wednesday 02.12**. DAI-TIC-C: **Tuesday 08.12**.
- **8 minutes** per group. Come 5 minutes before your slot, with your
  computer. A video projector is available.
- Present as you like, but:
  - show the client and the server **running**, including an error
    case,
  - explain the **protocol** and the choices behind it, not every line
    of code,
  - everyone speaks, and everyone can answer questions about the code.
- The timeslots are published on the practical work page once the
  groups are known.
:::

## Grading

- Each criterion: **0** (missing, off topic, or very little
  understanding), **0.1** (partially there, unclear or incomplete),
  **0.2** (complete, correct, clear understanding).
- Grade: 25 criteria × 0.2 = 5 points, + 1 = **6 maximum**.
- The good practices of PW1 (Git, GitHub, README, Maven) are expected;
  missing ones cost points (see the rules).

## How to test your protocol

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
- As in PW1, test the logic, not the network: a method takes the line
  received and returns the answer to send.
- The network code only reads lines, calls it, and writes the answers.
  The tests need no server and no client. With the SMS protocol:

```java
@Test
void answersAnUnknownMessageWithAnError() {
  Session session = new Session();
  assertEquals("ERROR -1", session.handle("HELLO"));
}

@Test
void refusesListBeforeJoin() {
  Session session = new Session();
  assertEquals("ERROR -2", session.handle("LIST"));
}
```
:::

## Rules: the team and the project (1/2)

- Everyone contributes, and the history shows it. Everyone can explain
  the whole project in detail, not only the part they wrote.
- A GitHub Discussion is opened **before the next course**, so that
  we can validate your idea.
- The network communication uses only the **Java classes of the
  course**. Any other library may serve the rest, the user interface
  for example. The README says which dependencies you use, and why.

## Rules: the team and the project (2/2)

- The application does **slightly more, and something slightly
  different**, than the course examples.
- The good practices of PW1 continue: issues, reviewed pull requests,
  descriptive and signed commits, the Maven wrapper, a clean
  `.gitignore`, a README that explains how to build and run it.
- It **builds and runs from a fresh clone**, with
  `./mvnw clean package`, on a machine that is not yours. What we cannot
  build, we cannot grade.

## Rules: the submission

- Discussion updated with the **repository link and the commit hash**
  before the deadline. We grade that commit, not what comes after it.
- **Private** repository: the teaching staff are collaborators. If we
  cannot open it at the deadline, the work counts as not submitted.
- Every started day of delay costs **1 point**.

## Rules: honesty and penalties

- State your sources: internet code, AI-generated code, ideas taken
  elsewhere. Say what you used them for (see the AI principles).
- Copying the code of another group gives a grade of **1** to everyone
  involved.
- Each rule not respected costs up to **1 point** on the final grade,
  and several can add up.

## Grades and feedback

- Your grade goes into GAPS.
- You receive an email with a comment for each criterion, a general
  comment on your work, and the grade.
- If anything is unclear, ask us.

## Tips

- **Keep it simple.** The Unix philosophy and KISS from PW1: a small
  protocol, well specified, with its errors handled, is worth more than
  an ambitious one that half works. Too complex may be penalized.
- **Make your image public.** A package on GitHub Container Registry
  starts **private**: **Package settings** > **Danger Zone** >
  **Change visibility** > **Public** (chapter 05).

## Tips: how and what to present

- **Presenting.** Slides, a live demo, a poster: as you like. Skip the
  objectives; show code only where it is interesting, complex or tricky.
  Focus on the **what** and the **why**, for someone who knows the course
  but not your project.

[Practical work 2](../practical-work/pw2.qmd) has everything: the demos,
the rules, the full grid.
